From a Secular and Liberal Environment to Islamic Values: The Influence of Liberal Thought versus the Rigidity of Conservatives

The emergence and development of the modern general education system have largely taken place under the influence of secular and liberal thought. Consequently, it is hardly realistic to expect that a person raised in such an educational system and environment will spontaneously develop a comprehensive understanding of Islamic values, beliefs, and worldview.

Nevertheless, even within this reality, those who strive to acquire Islamic knowledge, practise Islam to the best of their ability in their personal lives, and seek to contribute to the establishment of Islamic values in society and the state are undoubtedly demonstrating a positive and encouraging intellectual and moral transformation.

Therefore, it is not enough merely to acknowledge their sincere interest, efforts to change, and return to Islam as positive developments; it is also our religious and moral responsibility to welcome and appreciate these efforts wholeheartedly.

Their interest in Islam and their return to its teachings may extend beyond the transformation of their own lives. They may also become a source of inspiration for many others who have grown up within the general education system, encouraging them to rediscover Islamic values, beliefs, and injunctions.

However, two important and interrelated challenges arise in the process of this return to Islam. One emerges from within the Muslim community itself, while the other is associated with the intellectual and social environment in which those newly interested in Islam were previously raised.

Unless these two realities are properly understood, excessive rigidity towards newcomers may develop on the one hand, while, on the other, they may be inclined to reconcile Islam with elements of their previous intellectual outlook that are incompatible with Islamic teachings.

The first challenge concerns us. Those of us who adhere to relatively conservative Islamic thought sometimes tend to expect people who have recently become interested in Islamic values to undergo rapid and almost complete transformation.

In particular, greater emphasis is sometimes placed on outward changes—such as clothing, appearance, and visible patterns of social behaviour—than on the internal transformation of thought, belief, and values. When the expected changes do not become visible quickly enough, these individuals may face severe criticism, and their sincerity may even be called into question.

Yet changes in a person's thoughts, beliefs, values, and worldview are generally gradual processes that require time. The mental and intellectual framework developed over many years within a particular family, social, and educational environment cannot always be expected to change completely within a short period.

Excessive pressure, undue haste, and harsh criticism may, in fact, produce reactions opposite to those intended. A person who has approached Islam with sincerity and intellectual curiosity may become discouraged, and eventually their initial interest may begin to diminish.

Our approach towards those who are newly interested in Islam should therefore be characterised by patience, empathy, and a commitment to facilitating gradual transformation and providing opportunities for correction.

Rather than immediately criticising every shortcoming or deviation, it is more productive to allow them the opportunity to acquire the necessary knowledge and engage in self-correction. Merely pointing out their mistakes is not enough. A more constructive and responsible role is to accompany them on their journey towards positive change by providing sound knowledge, opportunities for spiritual purification, a supportive environment, and good examples to follow.

In particular, internal transformation should be regarded as the foundation of outward change. The deeper a person's understanding of and awareness of īmān (faith), ‘aqīdah (creed), the fundamental beliefs of Islam, and its obligatory and necessary injunctions become, the greater the possibility of lasting change in their practices and other aspects of life.

Outward transformation is certainly important. However, prioritising external changes without corresponding changes in inner belief, thought, and values may result in a transformation that is artificial or temporary. It may also risk overlooking the underlying foundations necessary for genuine and lasting change.

The Prophetic method of da‘wah also demonstrates wisdom and foresight in recognising the circumstances, preparedness, and psychological condition of those who were newly embracing Islam.

When a delegation from the tribe of Thaqīf approached the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) with the intention of accepting Islam, they presented certain conditions. Among them were that they should not be called upon to participate in military campaigns, that ‘ushr or zakāh should not be collected from their wealth, and that they should not be compelled to perform the prayer (ṣalāh).

Although the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) allowed some concessions regarding their conditions, he did not compromise on the matter of prayer. He said:

«لَكُمْ أَنْ لَا تُحْشَرُوا وَلَا تُعْشَرُوا، وَلَا خَيْرَ فِي دِينٍ لَيْسَ فِيهِ رُكُوعٌ»

“You may be exempted from being summoned for military campaigns and from having the prescribed levy collected from your wealth, but there is no good in a religion in which there is no bowing”—that is, no prayer.

— Sunan Abī Dāwūd

This incident points to an important principle in da‘wah and Islamic education. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) took into consideration the circumstances and level of preparedness of those who were newly embracing Islam, yet he did not compromise on its fundamental foundations.

In other words, the method of da‘wah may require wisdom, patience, and gradual progression, but there can be no compromise regarding the fundamental truths of Islam and its essential obligations.

The second challenge, by contrast, concerns the intellectual background of those who are newly interested in Islam. Having spent many years in the secular and liberal environment of the general education system, it is natural for some elements of their previous intellectual outlook to remain influential in their thinking and perspectives. The effects of years of education, social conditioning, and exposure to modern thought cannot be expected to disappear completely overnight.

As a result, they may sometimes attempt to understand or interpret various Islamic rulings, concepts, and social principles in ways that appear compatible with the intellectual framework they previously embraced.

Such reconsideration or reassessment is not necessarily negative in every instance. Indeed, examining the relationship between modern thought and Islamic teachings may be intellectually necessary for understanding contemporary realities.

The problem arises, however, when Islam is made to conform to a predetermined modern intellectual framework without an adequate understanding of its own sources, terminology, epistemological foundations, and established scholarly tradition.

Particular caution is therefore required here. Bringing Islam into dialogue with modern thought is one thing; attempting to make Islam conform to, or accommodate itself within, the predetermined standards of modern thought is quite another. The former may constitute a legitimate approach to intellectual inquiry, whereas the latter risks weakening Islam's distinctive epistemological and normative framework.

It is at this point that a psychological and intellectual tension may emerge between those newly interested in Islam and the more conservative Islamic milieu. On one side are the influences of their previous intellectual outlook; on the other are the expectations of the Islamic environment. Establishing a balance between these two realities is not easy. Both sides therefore need self-awareness, restraint, and a willingness to engage constructively.

Those who are newly embracing Islamic values must also recognise that, when examining the relationship between Islam and their previous intellectual outlook, it is not sound methodology to reinterpret Islam's fundamental beliefs, principles, or established epistemological and jurisprudential frameworks merely to make them conform to their pre-existing assumptions.

A profound understanding of Islam requires studying it in the light of its own sources, terminology, epistemological framework, and intellectual tradition. Questions may certainly be raised, and research may be undertaken, concerning the relationship between Islam and modern thought. However, such research must be grounded in sound Islamic knowledge.

For this reason, appropriate caution and restraint are also necessary when making pronouncements on Islamic intellectual, theoretical, philosophical, and jurisprudential matters. Presenting what is claimed to be Islam's “definitive position” on a particular issue cannot be justified merely by sincerity towards Islam or by a general reading of the Qur’an and Hadith.

It requires sustained and systematic study, adequate proficiency in the Arabic language, extensive knowledge of the Qur’an and Hadith, a thorough understanding of Uṣūl al-Fiqh and the jurisprudential tradition, and the ability to undertake comparative examination of different scholarly opinions and their supporting evidence.

The same principle applies to us. Knowing something about a particular subject does not automatically entitle us to make definitive pronouncements on every issue. Where specialised knowledge is required, relying on the opinions of qualified and experienced scholars in the relevant field is a normal scholarly practice. Respecting expertise and acknowledging the limits of one's own knowledge is not a weakness; rather, it is a hallmark of mature intellectual inquiry.

Accordingly, our appeal to those who are newly interested in Islamic values should be as follows:

Study Islam. Engage with the Qur’an and Hadith. Shape your thoughts and lives in the light of Islamic teachings. Put those teachings into practice, and contribute positively to efforts to establish Islamic values in society and the state.

At the same time, recognise the importance of appropriate qualifications and specialised expertise when making definitive pronouncements on complex intellectual, theoretical, and jurisprudential questions concerning Islam.

Those of us who consider ourselves adherents of conservative Islamic thought must also engage in self-criticism. Instead of expecting those who are newly approaching Islam to undergo complete transformation overnight, we should accompany them on their journey of learning, personal reform, and religious practice.

Their mistakes must be corrected, but not in a manner that destroys the very opportunity for correction. Their questions must be answered, but not in a way that discourages them from asking questions in the first place. Alongside encouraging their movement towards Islam, we must also help them become deeply acquainted with its fundamental teachings and established intellectual tradition.

Ultimately, our goal should not be merely the outward transformation of an individual, but a profound, knowledge-based, and lasting Islamic transformation of their thought, beliefs, moral character, and worldview. The deeper the inner transformation, the greater the likelihood that changes in outward conduct and religious practice will become more spontaneous and enduring.

Therefore, when dealing with people who are newly moving towards Islamic values and practice, we must avoid, on the one hand, the unnecessary haste, rigidity, and excessive emphasis on outward appearances that may characterise some conservative approaches.

On the other hand, those newly interested in Islam must remain conscious of the influence of their previous secular and liberal thinking and study Islam deeply in the light of its own sources and intellectual tradition.

One side needs patience and wisdom; the other needs self-awareness and intellectual discipline.
